notes.1a: The majority of candidates made a good start by correctly identifying four stakeholder groups such as Danielle and Anthony the owners, customers taking dance lessons, employees such as gym instructors, the finance manager and other businesses such as those selling dance shoes and clothing. Many responses then went on to explain the objective of each stakeholder. Some responses included Danielle and Anthony as two stakeholder groups and could only be given credit for one stakeholder group.
notes.1b: The answers to this question were generally good. Most responses discussed the advantages and disadvantages of three factors when deciding where to locate the dance studio. Strong responses demonstrated a recognition that most of their customers live near to the existing dance studio and therefore would need to be careful about moving too far away from them. Also, there was a need for a new larger building so that the business can expand. Better responses included detailed analysis earlier in the answer and then used this to compare the three factors before deciding which factor was the most important when deciding on the new location. Weaker responses were often repetitive, restating earlier points in the recommendation and hence gained no further credit or made a weak judgment selecting only one method to justify and gained some additional credit.
notes.2a: This question required candidates to identify and explain why well qualified employees are important for DADS business. Many answers discussed the benefits such as improved reputation, high quality classes and that injuries were less likely if classes were taught by well qualified teachers. The highest credit for this response was given to candidates who successfully related their explanation to the dance studio and gymnasium rather than those who gave a generic answer. The best responses gained full marks by fully applying the analysis to the business in the case study. �PAGE�19
notes.2b: Many candidates scored very well by calculating the current and acid test ratios for both years. Better candidates identified in the recommendation that the business had reduced liquidity and was in fact in danger of not being able to meet short-term debts. Weaker responses only considered what was happening to the figures, e.g. inventories fell by $200 or incorrectly calculated the ratios. Only the few best responses were applied to the business in the case study and were able to gain full credit.
notes.3a: Candidates often gave answers that recognised delegating to the new manager released time for Danielle and Anthony to make better use of their time on other areas of the business such as teaching classes. Many answers did not recognise that the finance manager was not qualified to carry out marketing functions and therefore may not make good decisions about marketing. The weaker responses did not demonstrate application or showed a lack of knowledge of what is meant by delegation, discussing instead the benefits and drawbacks of employing a new manager.
notes.3b: Many of the answers to this question were good. Most candidates could offer benefits of secondary research being cheap to collect but the other two methods being more expensive. Weaker responses were focused on competitors, existing customers and parents of children who attend classes rather than the three methods of market research being used. This approach often resulted in vague answers that did not go beyond level 1. Better responses gave a consideration of the advantages and disadvantages of each method of research and then justified which method of research was the best one, thus gaining some level 3 credit. Stronger responses justified why the alternative options were rejected, gaining further level 3 credit. Weaker responses simply repeated earlier points in the recommendation, such as by using questionnaires they would find out what customers wanted. A minority of responses discussed the use of the information rather than the methods of research, which was not the focus of the question. Application was present in many answers.
notes.4a: Many responses included lower unemployment and lower spending on health care but sometimes did not go on to apply the explanation to this context. Some responses wrote about the effects on the business of an increase in the number of dance studios, which was given no credit. Many answers were generic and so could only be given limited credit. Those candidates who applied their explanation of the external benefits to the increase in the number of dance studios gained the credit available for application.
notes.4b: This question was concerned with the effects of three changes on DADS. Many candidates identified that higher levels of employment might lead to higher incomes and consequently increased number of customers for the studio although it might be harder to find suitable employees leading to increased wage rates. While an increase in annual tax paid on buildings might result in DADS reconsidering the move to larger premises due to increased costs. Finally, as more children want to dance it might mean that DADS will need to expand or it will not be able to offer more classes and take on more customers, as many classes are full. A minority of responses incorrectly stated that a reduction in unemployment would lead to fewer customers. Better responses gave a conclusion of which change would have the greatest effect on DADS based on the earlier analysis and in the context of DADS. Weaker conclusions were usually a repetition of earlier statements and gained no further credit. Answers were often well applied by referring to the need to increase the size of the business so they do not have to turn away dancers and increasing the number of classes for adults as well as children, they also recognised that dance lessons were a luxury that may be paid for if incomes were rising from higher levels of employment leading to more customers for the dance studio and gymnasium.

(cid:127) Analytical skills are also tested through the case study examination. Candidates should try to give a full
explanation of positive and negative consequences of a business decision. This requires developed
reasoning rather than simple description; listed points generally only gain level 1 whereas an
explanation of a point could move the answer to level 2.
(cid:127) Several questions on this style of paper ask candidates to make justified recommendations. It is
important to offer a decision based on balanced argument without full repetition of the previous analysis.
The recommendation should compare and make reference as to why the other alternative options were
rejected as well as justifying the option that was chosen.
notes.general_comments:
Candidates had been generally well prepared for this examination with the strong performance of many
reflecting this. The context of Danielle and Anthony setting up a dance studio and gymnasium provided an
accessible scenario for most candidates. No question appeared to be too challenging. Time did not appear
to be a problem. Rarely did a candidate not to complete their answers in the one hour thirty minutes allowed.
The structure of the paper allowed candidates to demonstrate their knowledge of business concepts in the
first part (a) of each question. They were then expected to offer analysis and reasoning in answer to the
second part (b) of each question. This style of questioning has become standard practice on this particular
paper and it is good to see that many candidates are developing a strong examination technique and clearly
understand what is expected of them.
The layout of the examination paper provides side headings to prompt candidates in their responses.
Candidates should take careful note of how many marks are awarded for each question they should be quite
clear about the extent of developed detail that is required for each answer. Candidates could earn some
credit by defining business terms and using them confidently. Those who answered in the context of Danielle
and Anthony’s Dance Studio gained further credit.
The standard of written English was excellent. Candidates made themselves fully understood and are to be
congratulated on the high quality of spelling, punctuation and grammar offered in their responses. There is
no penalty for the wrong spelling of words or using incorrect punctuation.
Here are some points that might be helpful in enabling candidates to achieve most credit by using their
knowledge in an effective way.
(cid:127) Knowledge and understanding of balance sheets and liquidity ratios is part of the assessment in this
subject and candidates should prepare for a question, which will ask them about this topic.
0450 Business Studies June 2016
For example, look at the financial information in Appendix 2. Do you think DADS Is in a good
financial position? Justify your answer using liquidity ratios.
There are three levels of response to this answer where candidates are expected to calculate the
liquidity ratios for both years and analyse what the ratios show. Answers that simply offer generic
statements, such as – the current liabilities increased by $100 between 2014 and 2015 – would only be
rewarded with level 1 credit. Answers that correctly calculated the current and acid test ratio would earn
level 2 credit. Using the context of a dance studio and gymnasium to enhance the answer would gain up
to credit for application. In the final part of the answer, candidates are expected to evaluate the liquidity
position of the business and recognise that the liquidity has deteriorated between the two years. This
tests the candidates’ ability to calculate and then interpret the liquidity ratios and requires a clear
conclusion as to whether or not this business is in a good financial position.
(cid:127) In part (a) of each question there is a line for making a point and then a space below to explain or
develop the reasoning. Candidates should think carefully about the context of the business in the case
study before making their point and should ensure they do not repeat themselves in the explanation
For example, identify and explain two reasons why well qualified employees are important for
this business.
Some credit will be given for demonstrating knowledge of two reasons for employing well qualified
employees such as it will give the business a better reputation, ensure higher quality classes or be less
likely to have customers injure themselves. A weak explanation might follow that well qualified
employees will ensure good quality classes. However, a better explanation made clear that good quality
classes will lead to a good reputation for the dance studio encouraging dancers to tell their friends
leading to more people wanting to join the classes. There could then be higher revenue and possibly
higher profit for the partnership. Children will improve their dancing skills and move to higher level
classes more quickly as they are taught by highly qualified teachers.
